source_title: Obstructing a Peace Officer, Firefighter, EMS Provider, Rescue Specialist, or Volunteer (drone-specific provision)
uas_topic: Interference with emergency/public-safety operations by UAS
regulated_activity: Using or threatening to use a UAS as an 'obstacle' to obstruct, impair, or hinder a peace officer, firefighter, EMS provider, rescue specialist, or volunteer acting under official authority
permit_or_approval_required: No general permit; conditional exception requires coordination with the responding agency
summary: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 18-8-104 defines 'obstacle' to include an unmanned aircraft system (§ (5)(b)). A person commits the offense by using or threatening to use a UAS as an obstacle to knowingly obstruct, impair, or hinder a peace officer, firefighter, EMS provider, rescue specialist, or volunteer acting under color of official authority. Subsection (2.5) provides that the offense does not apply if the UAS operator (a) obtains permission to operate from the law enforcement agency or entity coordinating the emergency response, (b) continues to communicate with that entity during operation, and (c) immediately complies with any instructions concerning the UAS's operation. The offense is a class 2 misdemeanor (up to 120 days imprisonment and/or a fine up to $750).
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not fly at or near an active emergency, accident, or wildfire scene without first obtaining permission from the coordinating law enforcement or incident-command entity and maintaining communication with them throughout the flight — this is directly relevant to any AEC post-disaster damage assessment or infrastructure-inspection flight near an active incident.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Before any planned UAS work near an active emergency response, establish contact with the law-enforcement, fire, EMS, or incident-command entity coordinating the scene and ask how it grants operating permission and maintains in-flight communications. Retain the permission and communication plan, brief the pilot on immediate-compliance expectations, and do not assume a client request substitutes for response-agency coordination.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the specific permission obtained from the coordinating entity (agency name, contact, time granted) before and during any flight near an active emergency response, since the statutory exception is conditioned on ongoing communication and compliance, not merely initial permission; retain this documentation given the misdemeanor exposure.
verification_status: Full current statutory text (including the 2018 UAS amendment and 2021 subsection (1.5) addition) verified directly against Justia's codification of the Colorado Revised Statutes.

source_title: Criminal Invasion of Privacy (camera-agnostic; applies to drone-mounted cameras)
uas_topic: Privacy / unauthorized surveillance by UAS-mounted camera
regulated_activity: Knowingly observing or photographing another person's intimate parts, without consent, where the person observed/photographed has a reasonable expectation of privacy
summary: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 18-7-801 makes it a class 2 misdemeanor to knowingly observe or photograph another person's intimate parts (as defined in § 18-3-401(2)) without consent, in a situation where the person has a reasonable expectation of privacy. The statute is camera-agnostic — it does not reference drones by name — but its definition of 'photograph' expressly includes photographs, motion pictures, videotape, live feed, and other electronically or digitally reproduced visual material, which industry commentary and secondary sources describe as applying to drone-mounted camera surveillance.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Routine AEC aerial mapping, inspection, and construction-progress photography is far outside the conduct this statute targets, but avoid incidental capture of private outdoor spaces (yards, pools, windows) where individuals might have a reasonable expectation of privacy, and adjust flight paths or camera angles near residential areas accordingly.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This is an intent-based statute requiring knowing observation of intimate parts specifically, not general aerial photography — document the professional/survey purpose of a flight if a project boundary abuts residential property, but this statute presents low practical risk for standard commercial AEC UAS work.
verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against Justia's codification of the Colorado Revised Statutes; the statute's application specifically to drones (as opposed to cameras generally) is confirmed only via secondary industry-compliance sources, not by a Colorado court decision located in this research pass.

source_title: Landowner Airspace Rights and Civil Trespass
uas_topic: Civil trespass / landowner airspace rights applicable to UAS overflight
regulated_activity: Operating an aircraft (including, per secondary sources, a UAS) over private property in a manner that interferes with the landowner's use and enjoyment
summary: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 41-1-107 recognizes a surface landowner's interest in the airspace above their land, providing a statutory basis for civil trespass claims arising from intrusive overflights. Federal law controls the navigable airspace itself, but this statute addresses civil liability for overflights that unreasonably interfere with a landowner's use and enjoyment of their property. Secondary industry-compliance sources describe this as the primary Colorado statutory hook for drone-overflight civil-trespass claims, alongside common-law intrusion-upon-seclusion theories.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Obtain landowner consent or a documented right of access before flying low-altitude survey or inspection missions over adjacent private parcels outside the project boundary, since repeated or low overflight could support a civil trespass claim even without any criminal violation.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This is a civil-liability statute, not a licensing or permitting requirement — advise clients that a civil trespass claim is a real risk distinct from FAA compliance and the criminal statutes above; the exact contours of 'interference' sufficient to support a claim have not been independently verified against Colorado case law in this pass.
verification_status: Full current statutory text of Colo. Rev. Stat. § 41-1-107 directly fetched and read against Justia's codification in this retrofit pass, confirming the exact operative language ('The ownership of space above the lands and waters of this state is declared to be vested in the several owners of the surface beneath, subject to the right of flight of aircraft'). Previously cited only to a secondary compilation source (dronelaws.us); that citation has been replaced.

geographic_scope: Statewide (CPW-administered state parks and outdoor recreation lands)
source_title: Prohibition on Manned-Aircraft Landing/Takeoff on State Parks and Outdoor Recreation Lands (no verifiable UAS-specific subsection located)
citation: 2 C.C.R. 405-1, Chapter P-1, Article I, Regulation #100.b.15 (the only 'aircraft' provision confirmed present in CPW's own currently-published regulation text; the widely-recirculated 'Regulation #100.c.24' UAS-specific citation could not be verified against any primary CPW source)
effective_date: Chapter P-1 effective May 1, 2017 (text obtained); UAS-specific subsection reported effective Jan. 1, 2018 per secondary sources
revision_date: Unknown — regulation text obtained reflects the 2017 adoption; a later UAS-specific amendment is reported but not independently confirmed
status: Current / in force (the confirmed #100.b.15 manned-aircraft provision); the reported UAS-specific subsection remains unverified
uas_topic: State park/outdoor recreation land UAS restriction
regulated_activity: Launching, landing, or operating a UAS on Colorado state parks, state wildlife areas, or state trust lands administered by CPW
requirement_type: Prohibition, except in designated model-aircraft areas
summary: CPW's own published Chapter P-1 regulation (2 CCR 405-1, effective May 1, 2017, and by its own terms remaining in force until repealed, amended, or superseded) was fetched and read in full directly from cpw.state.co.us in this retrofit pass. It prohibits landing or taking off with any 'aircraft' on Parks and Outdoor Recreation Lands and waters absent specific authorization or an emergency (#100.b.15); 'aircraft' is expressly defined there as a device used or intended for manned flight or to otherwise hold humans aloft (airplanes, helicopters, gliders, hot air balloons, hang gliders, parachutes, parasails, kite boards, kite tubes, zip lines, and similar devices/equipment) -- this definition does not on its face include unmanned/UAS devices, and the regulation's full text (all of Articles I, II, and IV) contains no separate UAS-specific subsection. A UAS-specific prohibition -- consistently cited by numerous secondary drone-law compilation sites (dronelaws.us, flyusi.org, pilotinstitute.com, uavcoach.com, dronesgator.com, propelrc.com) as 'Regulation #100-c.24,' effective January 1, 2018 -- could not be located in CPW's own currently-published regulation text in either this pass or the original research pass. None of the secondary sources repeating this citation point to a primary CPW document, and the citation format itself (#100-c.24) does not match Chapter P-1's actual subsection-lettering scheme (#100 has subsections a. through j., with 'c' not existing at all -- the document runs a./b. directly into camping/littering/etc. under b., then d./e./f./g./h./i./j.). This pattern -- an unsourced citation repeated verbatim across many mutually-reinforcing secondary compilation sites with no primary document ever cited -- is treated in this project as a red flag for citation-chain fabrication or drift rather than as a verified UAS-specific rule.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Continue to treat CPW-administered state parks, state wildlife areas, and state trust lands as effectively off-limits for UAS launch/landing/operation as a conservative operating posture, but do not represent 'Regulation #100-c.24' to a client as a verified citation -- it could not be confirmed against CPW's own published regulation text in two independent research passes. The only confirmed binding text (#100.b.15) targets manned aircraft; CPW may still enforce against UAS operators under general trespass, unauthorized-use, or resource-protection theories even absent a UAS-specific aircraft subsection, so the practical no-fly recommendation is unchanged even though its cited legal basis has been corrected.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Advise the client that the frequently-cited 'CPW Regulation #100-c.24' cannot currently be verified as an existing provision of Colorado's Code of Regulations based on a direct, full read of CPW's own published Chapter P-1 text; recommend written confirmation directly from CPW's Office of the Regulations Manager (1313 Sherman, Room 111, Denver, CO 80203) before either relying on or discounting a UAS-specific state-park prohibition for a specific project, and note that the confirmed manned-aircraft provision (#100.b.15) does not itself reach UAS by its own terms.
verification_status: The full current text of CPW Chapter P-1 (2 CCR 405-1), all Articles, was fetched and read directly from cpw.state.co.us in this retrofit pass (a more thorough re-verification than the original pass, which read #100.b.15 only). This confirms no UAS-specific subsection currently exists in CPW's own published document, and that the secondary-source citation 'Regulation #100-c.24' does not match the document's actual structure. This is a negative/corrective finding about the citation, not a finding that CPW permits UAS activity on its lands -- the practical guidance remains cautious pending direct CPW confirmation.
notes: Material correction from the original research pass: the discrepancy previously flagged as unresolved has been more precisely characterized -- 'Regulation #100.c.24' is very likely a fabricated or drifted citation with no primary source, not an amendment CPW simply failed to include in an older PDF copy. Recommend direct written confirmation from CPW before a specific client engagement turns on this point.

source_title: Prohibition on Using UAS to Aid in Hunting or Wildlife Detection/Scouting
citation: 2 C.C.R. 406-0, Chapter W-0, Article IV, #004(C) (confirmed via direct fetch of the current rule text)
regulated_activity: Using a UAS, or any remotely guided device, to search for, scout, or detect wildlife to aid in hunting or the taking of wildlife
summary: The current text of 2 CCR 406-0 (Colorado Parks and Wildlife Commission regulations), Article IV #004(C), was fetched and read directly from the Colorado Secretary of State's CCR database in this retrofit pass. It provides: 'It shall be unlawful to use a drone to look for, scout, or detect wildlife as an aid in the hunting or taking of wildlife,' with 'drone' defined at #004(C)(1) as 'any contrivance invented, used or designed for navigation of, or flight in the air that is unmanned or guided remotely,' also referred to as an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) or Unmanned Aerial Vehicle System (UAVS). This confirms the effective January 1, 2018 prohibition on drone-aided hunting/scouting and the underlying citation exactly. Reported penalties under Colorado's 'Samson Law' wildlife-value framework (from $70 for small game up to $125,000 for trophy species) were not independently re-verified against the primary penalty schedule in this pass but were consistent with the Colorado Legislative Council Staff's October 2024 issue brief cited previously.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Plan environmental-monitoring, habitat-mapping, or resource-inventory UAS flights to avoid any activity that could be read as searching for, scouting, or detecting wildlife for hunting purposes, and build a conservative standoff buffer near known wildlife concentrations to avoid a harassment finding, particularly during hunting seasons.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the survey/mapping purpose of any UAS flight over wildlife habitat to distinguish it from a hunting-related use; CPW has been reported to actively monitor social media for evidence of violations, so retain flight logs and mission documentation establishing a non-hunting purpose.
verification_status: Full current rule text of 2 CCR 406-0, Article IV #004(C), including the operative prohibition and the drone/UAV/UAVS definition, fetched and read directly against the Colorado Secretary of State's official CCR database (sos.state.co.us) in this retrofit pass -- superseding the prior pass's secondary-source-only citation (dronelaws.us).

source_title: SB26-024 — 'Unmanned Aircraft Systems Rights and Authorities Act' (Postponed Indefinitely, Not Enacted)
citation: Colo. SB26-024 (2026 Regular Session, 75th General Assembly), introduced 01/14/2026
source_type: Proposed or pending authority — postponed indefinitely (dead); not currently binding
status: Postponed indefinitely by Senate Local Government & Housing Committee, Feb. 25, 2026; not enacted
uas_topic: Proposed comprehensive state/local UAS regulatory framework
regulated_party: Individuals, commercial UAS operators, the state, and local governments
regulated_activity: Proposed: authorizing recreational and lawful commercial drone operation statewide; limiting local-government regulatory authority over drone ownership/operation/design/manufacture/testing/maintenance/licensing/registration/certification/equipment and pilot qualifications; preserving local authority over drones the locality itself owns/uses or that launch/land on its property, and over generally applicable nuisance-type ordinances
aec_relevance: Moderate (would have been high if enacted — would have functioned similarly to Texas's § 423.009 local preemption)
summary: SB26-024, introduced January 14, 2026 by Sen. Liston, Sen. Michaelson Jenet, and Rep. Soper, would have created the 'Unmanned Aircraft Systems Rights and Authorities Act.' As introduced, the bill would have authorized recreational drone operation statewide and commercial drone operation where the underlying business is lawful and the operation complies with state and federal law; prohibited the state or a political subdivision from requiring UAS registration beyond state/federal requirements; clarified that federal-law-compliant operation does not by itself create legal liability; and established and limited both state and local regulatory authority — local governments would have retained authority only over drones they own/operate, drones launching/landing on their own property, and generally applicable ordinances (e.g., nuisance regulations), while losing authority to independently regulate UAS ownership, operation, design, manufacture, testing, maintenance, licensing, registration, certification, equipment, or pilot training/certification. The Senate Local Government & Housing Committee adopted twelve amendments on February 25, 2026, but then voted 5-2 to postpone the bill indefinitely, killing it for the 2026 session.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not rely on SB26-024 for any current compliance purpose — it did not pass and Colorado's current local-ordinance patchwork (see CO-007) remains in full force. Monitor for reintroduction in a future session, since this bill's approach (state framework limiting local regulatory scope while preserving local property-based and nuisance authority) closely tracks reforms enacted in other states and could reduce local-ordinance complexity if it passes in a later session.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Advise clients that no Colorado bill currently limits local UAS regulatory authority; if SB26-024 or a similar successor bill is reintroduced and passes in a future session, revisit the local-ordinance research category (CO-007) since the compliance landscape would change materially.
verification_status: Bill status, sponsor information, amendment history, and the Feb. 25, 2026 postpone-indefinitely vote (5-2) confirmed directly against the Colorado General Assembly's official bill-tracking page; the full introduced bill text (PDF) was not independently read in full in this pass, so the summary above is based on the official bill-summary language on that page rather than a full read of the statutory text as introduced.

summary: HB 17-1070 (2017) directed the Center of Excellence for Advanced Technology Aerial Firefighting, within the Colorado Department of Public Safety, to study ways to safely integrate UAS into state and local government functions relating to firefighting, search and rescue, accident reconstruction, crime-scene documentation, emergency management, and emergencies involving significant property loss, injury, or death, and established a pilot program for UAS deployment to fire-hazard regions. SB 19-020 (codified at § 24-33.5-1228, C.R.S.) provided ongoing funding for the CoE to develop a system to patrol the airspace above wildland fires using drones. The CoE has continued researching and testing UAS use for public-safety purposes, publishing findings on its Unmanned Aerial Systems webpage.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This program governs state/local government UAS operations rather than private commercial operators directly, but AEC firms performing wildfire-related mapping, damage assessment, or infrastructure-inspection work for a Colorado state or local public-safety agency should coordinate directly with the CoE or the relevant agency's UAS program to deconflict airspace, particularly during active wildfire response when TFRs are in effect.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Confirm whether a specific state or local government contract incorporates CoE protocols or airspace-deconfliction requirements as binding contract terms; this is a program-administration record rather than a private-operator compliance requirement, but is relevant context for any AEC work performed on behalf of, or adjacent to, Colorado public-safety UAS operations.

issuing_authority: Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies (DORA) — State Board of Licensure for Architects, Professional Engineers and Professional Land Surveyors
source_title: General Professional-Practice Competency Requirement (no UAS-specific board guidance located)
citation: Colo. Rev. Stat. Title 12, Article 120 (Professional Engineers and Professional Land Surveyors) — general competency-in-practice framework
binding_level: Binding (general only — no UAS-specific rule or guidance identified)
regulated_activity: Practicing only in fields in which the licensee is competent by education/experience
summary: Colorado's licensing framework for professional engineers and professional land surveyors (Title 12, Article 120, C.R.S., administered by DORA's State Board of Licensure for Architects, Professional Engineers and Professional Land Surveyors) requires licensees to practice only in fields in which they are, by education and/or experience, competent and proficient. No standalone Colorado-specific board rule, advisory, or guidance document addressing UAS-derived photogrammetry, LiDAR, or mapping products was located during this research pass. A frequently-cited secondary source describing a 'Rule 415' competency standard and applying it specifically to UAS mapping work was found to reference California's Board of Registration for Professional Engineers, Land Surveyors and Geologists and California's Land Surveyor's Act (Section 8726) rather than Colorado law, and should not be relied upon as a Colorado-specific citation.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Route UAS-derived photogrammetry/LiDAR mapping products through a Colorado-licensed PE or PLS for review under the existing general competency framework before delivery on any official survey or engineering deliverable, since no Colorado-specific UAS board standard currently exists to follow instead.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document licensed-professional review and QA/QC of UAS-derived deliverables given the absence of Colorado-specific UAS guidance; do not cite the 'Rule 415' language found in some secondary sources as a Colorado authority, since it traces to California's licensing framework rather than Colorado's Title 12, Article 120 framework.
verification_status: General Title 12, Article 120 competency-in-practice framework re-confirmed directly against Justia's current codification in this retrofit pass (replacing the prior FindLaw citation). A fresh, independent search for Colorado-specific DORA/State Board of Licensure UAS or drone-photogrammetry guidance (including the 3 CCR 720 rule series) was re-run in this pass and again found none -- the negative finding is now corroborated by two independent research passes rather than one, which supports the confidence upgrade from Low to Moderate. The previously-identified 'Rule 415' citation continues to trace to California's licensing framework rather than Colorado's.
notes: Recommend direct confirmation with DORA's Division of Professions and Occupations (dora_dpo_licensing@state.co.us) before representing to a client that no Colorado-specific UAS competency standard exists, consistent with the general no-negative-finding-is-ever-fully-conclusive caveat applied elsewhere in this project.
